In the French Romantic model the two sets cross near the vertical midpoint, so that both hands can reach both sets at the point of greatest resonance; in the Spanish type they cross near the neck. Contemporary instruments use gut, nylon or metal strings, from about two to more than five octaves; a six-by-six layout has six strings in each row and covers a wider range at the same size than a seven-by-five layout. The soundbox is smaller and the string tension lighter, and the source does not describe how volume is controlled.

Contemporary instruments mostly follow Celtic or folk forms, and there are recordings made specifically for the cross-strung harp, which shows that it has entered the recording studio.
交叉弦豎琴最早可追溯至十六世紀末西班牙的 arpa de dos órdenes: The cross-strung harp goes back at most to the Spanish arpa de dos órdenes of the late sixteenth century; by the early seventeenth century it had an established identity and was used for liturgical and secular music, and Bartolomé Jovernardi described it and invented a chromatic variant. Its popularity peaked at the end of the seventeenth century and then declined as Italian and French instruments displaced Spanish court music. At the end of the nineteenth century the harpe chromatique, designed on the proportions of the pedal harp, appeared in Paris, its two sets of strings crossing at the middle of their length so that both hands could reach the point of greatest resonance; there were related developments in Belgium and the United States. In 1987 the contemporary revival began in California.

The cross-strung harp (Hornbostel–Sachs 322.212.2) is a chordophone, a multi-row harp whose two rows of strings cross without touching, each of the twelve semitones having its own string. The player plucks with both hands and gets the semitones without pedals or levers. The early Spanish arpa de dos órdenes was used for liturgical and secular music; in nineteenth-century Paris Pleyel's harpe chromatique was made for orchestral use, and Claude Debussy's Danses sacrée et profane was written for harp and strings. Today it is found in folk harp playing and on recordings.
演奏者以雙手取用兩排交叉但不相觸的弦；兩排合起來提供十二個半音，每音各有一弦。現: The player takes the two crossing rows, which do not touch, with both hands; together the rows supply the twelve semitones, one string for each. The common modern seven-by-five layout puts the seven natural notes in one row and the five accidentals in the other, with a fingering like a keyboard: each major key has its fixed pattern, and the basic chords also group together. Beginners can learn the natural-note row, the main row, first, then practise taking notes across both rows with either hand.
